name: Superliving
tagline: Habit and wellbeing app built around small daily actions, challenges and team programs, usually paid for by an employer.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified. Consumer tier and employer licensing are not confirmed here.

verdictSummary: The mechanical core, pick habits, check them off, see streaks and a weekly score, is one of the most solved problems in software and an agent will hand you a working version before lunch. What you cannot generate is the content layer: the curated habit library, the nudges written by people who study behaviour change, and the structured programs that give the app its opinion about what you should do. If your copy is employer-provided, the team challenges and shared leaderboards are the actual product and a solo build replaces none of that. As a private tracker for someone who already knows which habits they want, the DIY version is genuinely fine. As a replacement for a workplace wellbeing program, it is not the same object.
coreLoopDIY: A local-first habit tracker where you define habits, tick them daily, and see streaks plus a rolling weekly completion score.
requirements: A browser that supports installing a PWA if you want it on your phone home screen
whatYouLose: The curated habit and program content, which is most of what you were paying for
Team challenges, leaderboards and whatever social pressure actually made you check the box
Push notifications that reliably fire on iOS
Cross-device sync without you standing up a backend
Any aggregate reporting an employer or coach was reading
moatNotes: The behaviour-change content and the employer distribution channel are the durable parts. The checkbox UI is not.
whyPeopleStillPay: Mostly because someone else is paying: these apps land on your phone through an HR wellbeing budget, and the value proposition is aimed at the buyer, not you. For individual users the honest answer is that a habit tracker only works if something outside the app keeps you opening it, and curated programs plus visible teammates do that better than a spreadsheet you wrote yourself. A self-built tracker gets used enthusiastically for eleven days.
notes: Building the tracker is trivial; sticking with it is the hard part, and that is exactly the part you cannot code.
prompt:
Build a local-first personal habit tracker as an installable PWA. No accounts, no backend, no telemetry.

Stack, non negotiable:
- Vite + React + TypeScript
- Tailwind for styling
- Dexie (IndexedDB) for all storage, everything stays on device
- vite-plugin-pwa for the manifest and service worker

Data model:
- Habit: id, name, emoji, cadence ('daily' | 'weekdays' | 'n-per-week' with target), colour, archived flag, createdAt
- Entry: id, habitId, date (YYYY-MM-DD local), done boolean, optional short note

Screens, three total:
1. Today: list of habits due today with big tap targets, tap to toggle done, long press or a small icon to add a note. Show current streak per habit.
2. History: per habit, a 12 week grid of small squares coloured by completion, plus current streak, longest streak, and completion rate over the last 30 days.
3. Habits: create, edit, reorder, archive. Archiving keeps history, never deletes entries.

Also build:
- A weekly score on Today: completed required checks divided by required checks for the current week, shown as a percentage and a single sentence of plain feedback, no motivational filler.
- Export and import all data as a single JSON file, with a confirm step on import.
- Dark mode following the OS setting.

Explicitly out of scope: sync, sharing, leaderboards, reminders via server push, AI coaching, any curated habit library. Ship a local notification via the Notification API only if permission is granted, and make it clear in the UI that it is unreliable when the app is closed.

Seed the database on first run with three example habits so the UI is never empty, and include a visible 'clear seed data' button.

Deliver a README with dev, build and preview commands, and no .env since there are no secrets.
